title: PARTNERING WITH AI: A PEDAGOGICAL FEEDBACK SYSTEM FOR LLM INTEGRATION INTO PROGRAMMING EDUCATION
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language models (LLMs) can be used to provide pedagogically sound feedback in programming education, rather than simply generating generic automated hints. The authors argue that prior LLM feedback systems in programming often overlook established pedagogical principles such as adapting feedback to student mastery, task progress, and the nature of students’ help requests. Their research questions focus on how to design an LLM-based feedback system aligned with pedagogical theory and how such feedback compares with human teacher feedback.

To study this, the authors first conducted a preliminary interview with one secondary-school computer science teacher to identify useful adaptation criteria for feedback. They then developed a pedagogical framework that conditions LLM feedback on task description, student mastery, student attempt, and optional student text input. The framework was implemented in a web-based Python programming application using GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini, with multiple specialized agents for error analysis, teacher-style feedback generation, and pedagogical validation. The system was evaluated using a mixed-methods design with semi-structured interviews and rating tasks.

The population consisted of eight secondary-school computer science teachers in Germany who had experience teaching Python across grades spanning roughly middle and high school. Teachers interacted with the system and evaluated pre-generated LLM feedback responses to synthetic student programming requests based on recursion tasks. The evaluation included both qualitative interview data and quantitative ratings of correctness, pedagogical soundness, comprehensiveness, effectiveness, comparison to teachers’ own feedback, and need for edits.

The main conclusions are that teachers generally viewed the LLM-generated feedback as pedagogically sound, understandable, and effective when it was structured according to the proposed framework. Teachers especially valued the speed and precision of LLMs for error detection and their potential to support both high- and low-performing students. At the same time, the study found important limitations: LLMs could not adapt well to dynamic classroom context, lacked interactive real-time awareness of student thinking, and could not use the visual and situational teaching strategies that human teachers employ. The authors conclude that LLMs are best understood as complements to, rather than replacements for, teachers in programming feedback.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-method qualitative study with small-sample teacher evaluations (n=8) using synthetic student scenarios rather than direct student outcome data. It provides useful practitioner evidence but lacks causal student-learning estimates and has limited external validity.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests promising but unclear impact, based mainly on teacher perceptions of pedagogical quality and efficiency rather than measured student effects. Positive signals exist, but no direct effect size on learner outcomes is reported.

interventions.use_case: LLM-driven pedagogical feedback generation for secondary-school Python programming tasks, using adaptive prompts and multi-agent validation to provide mastery- and progress-sensitive code feedback.
Conversational help interface embedded in a web-based programming practice tool where students request support and receive LLM-generated responses tailored to coding attempts and questions.

finding.finding_summary: The study did not measure student learning gains directly; instead, eight German secondary computer science teachers evaluated pre-generated LLM feedback on recursion tasks. Teachers rated responses as generally pedagogically sound (Mean=3.84, SD=1.10), comprehensive (Mean=4.04, SD=1.01), and effective for supporting learning (Mean=3.89, SD=1.14), but qualitative data emphasized important limits in contextual adaptation and classroom responsiveness.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of pedagogical soundness, comprehensiveness, effectiveness, and qualitative interview judgments about support for programming learning
finding.study_size: n=8 teachers; 60 sampled requests/responses discussed from a mock dataset of 329
finding.std_deviation: Pedagogical soundness SD=1.10; comprehensiveness SD=1.01; effectiveness SD=1.14

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived the LLM feedback system as more efficient than human teachers for routine error detection and timely support, especially for identifying small code errors quickly and providing parallel assistance in larger classes. Accuracy judgments were high, with 91.7% of evaluated responses rated correct and 8.3% partially correct, though these are perception-based rather than direct workflow productivity measurements.
finding.measure: Teacher judgments of correctness and qualitative perceptions of speed, precision, and ability to reduce teacher workload through instant feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLM feedback systems can complement teachers and may help address class-size and support-all-students challenges, but teachers also stressed that these systems cannot replace human expertise because they lack situational awareness and alignment with classroom context. Findings therefore support augmentation rather than substitution at the classroom-system level.
finding.measure: Teacher interview perceptions about fit with classroom practice, scalability, and role of AI versus teachers
